x: Accept AUR payments (merchant guide) How a shop, a game or a service can take payments in AUR and know they are final. The idea You create a wallet that only receives. For each order, you give the customer your address and an amount (and an order ID you track yourself). You watch the chain for a payment that matches. When it shows as confirmed, it is final: AUREN has no reorganisations once a block is confirmed. Use a name as your payment address Register a name like myshop.aur ( Names ). Customers can pay the name instead of a long address, and their wallet checks it for them. Watch for payments Poll the account's recent activity: or with the SDK: Matching payments to orders A transfer has no memo field. The simplest reliable ways: One address per order. Derive a fresh address for each customer. The payment tells you the order. Unique amounts. Ask for 10.000137 AUR where the last digits identify the order. Names. Give each customer a sub-account name like order123.myshop . (Register an ending you own and keep it restricted.) Confirmations A payment is final as soon as its block is confirmed, usually within a few seconds. There is nothing to wait for beyond that. Check receipt.status === 1 (the payment succeeded) and that the amount and recipient match. Refunds Send a normal transfer back to the from address of the payment. Safety Keep the receiving wallet's recovery key offline. For withdrawals use a separate wallet with a daily limit and trusted helpers ( Wallet guide ). Run your own node for production so you do not depend on someone else's. Pin the network's genesis hash ( Integrate ). Never accept a payment as final from a transaction that is only "waiting".

h: The pieces | A payment, step by step | Consensus | Fees: the adaptive market | Parallel execution | Accounts and keys | Money | Names | Smart contracts | Governance | Networks | Trust model in one paragraph
x: How AUREN works (architecture) A guided tour of the pieces, from a button press in the wallet to a confirmed block. The pieces Piece What it is Where Wallet Holds keys, builds and signs payments. Runs in a browser, a Windows app or an Android app. website/wallet.js , apps Node A program that keeps a full copy of the chain, checks every block and answers requests. src/node.js Validators Nodes that also propose and sign blocks. They are chosen by stake. src/consensus.js , src/bft.js Chain The rules: accounts, fees, staking, names, governance, smart contracts. src/chain.js , src/tx.js Explorer A website that reads from a node and shows everything. website/explorer.js Faucet On test networks, a small service that gives coins away. bin/auren-faucet.js A payment, step by step Build. The wallet asks a node for your payment number (nonce) and the current fee, and writes a transaction. Preview. It sends the transaction to the node's aur_simulate , which runs it against the current state without changing anything and returns the exact effect and fee. You see this on the Review screen. Sign. The wallet signs with your key, on your device. The key never leaves it. Submit. The signed transaction goes to a node ( aur_sendTx ). The node checks the signature, nonce and fee, adds it to its waiting list (the mempool) and tells its peers. Propose. Validators take turns. The chosen validator for this height packs waiting transactions into a block, ordered by fee. Vote. Validators vote in two rounds (prevote, precommit). With more than two thirds of voting power, the block is final. There is no "wait for six confirmations". Execute. Every node runs the block with the same code and gets the same result, byte for byte. The block header commits to the resulting state, so any difference is detected at once. Confirm. The wallet polls the node and shows "confirmed". Consensus AUREN uses a two-phase Byzantine fault tolerant proof-of-stake protocol: a block needs signatures from more than two thirds of the voting power. Validators that sign two different blocks at the same height are penalised and removed. Details: Consensus . Fees: the adaptive market Two resources are priced separately: compute (how much work) and state (how much is stored). Each has a fee level that rises when blocks are more than half full and falls when they are empty, within limits. The fee is burned. Because the two are separate, a storage-heavy action cannot make plain payments expensive. Details: Fee market . Parallel execution Transactions that touch different accounts run side by side in lanes. Every transaction declares which parts of the state it touches, so the node can prove which ones are independent. The result is identical to running them one by one. Smart-contract calls and name registrations under user-created endings run alone because they touch shared state. Accounts and keys An account is an address derived from a public key. Software wallets use Ed25519; phone and security-key wallets use ECDSA P-256 (WebAuthn); Ethereum wallets use secp256k1. Accounts can add trusted helpers, a delay for weakening settings and a daily limit, enforced by every validator. Details: Account security . Money New AUR is issued every block, starting at 3% a year and falling to 0.5%. Validators and their stakers get most of it; 10% goes to the node-reward pool. Fees and penalties are burned. Details: Tokenomics , Node rewards . Names Names like alice.aur live on the chain as records. A node answers a lookup with a Merkle proof, so a light client can check the answer against the validator set without trusting the node. Anyone can create their own name ending (TLD). Details: Names , Name resolution . Smart contracts An Ethereum-compatible virtual machine runs contracts. The Ethereum JSON-RPC is available on every node, so Ethereum tools work with a different chain ID. Details: EVM . Governance People who stake vote on proposals that change a whitelist of network settings. A passed proposal waits for a timelock before it applies. Details: Governance . Networks One mainnet, one testnet and one devnet. Each is identified by its genesis file; the genesis hash is pinned in networks/networks.json so wallets can detect a wrong network. Details: Networks . Trust model in one paragraph You trust your own device and the code you run. You do not have to trust any single node: payments are checked by the whole network, name answers come with proofs, and the genesis hash pins the chain. If a node lies, other nodes and your own checks catch it.

x: Build a wallet app A checklist and walkthrough for making your own wallet on AUREN, in any language. What a wallet must do Make and store keys safely. Show a balance and activity. Send payments with a preview. Receive (show an address). Optionally: staking, names, security settings. 1. Keys Generate 32 random bytes (the seed). From it make an Ed25519 key pair. The address is Bech32 of the scheme byte and the first 20 bytes of sha256(scheme ‖ public key) with the network prefix ( aur , taur , daur ). The same seed works on all networks; only the prefix differs. Details and code: Integrate . Store the seed encrypted with a user password (a slow password hash such as PBKDF2 or Argon2, then AES-GCM). Offer a printed recovery key. Never send it anywhere or write it to logs. Device keys (passkeys, security keys) use scheme 2. The private key never leaves the device and signing goes through WebAuthn. 2. Connect Let the user pick Devnet, Testnet or Mainnet. Ask a node for aur_status . Check status.network matches what the user picked, and refuse to continue if not. Pin the genesis hash from networks/networks.json . 3. Balance and activity Show spendable as the headline number. Show amounts in AUR, never sparks. 4. Send with a preview Always preview with aur_simulate and show the fee and result. If sim.ok is false, show the reason and do not send. 5. Names Before paying a name, resolve it with aur_resolve and verify the proof ( website/anr.js ). If the same name gives different addresses on different networks, refuse and ask for the address. Show the verified name next to the address the user is paying. 6. Receive Show the address with a copy button. Optionally a QR code. On test networks add a faucet button ( POST /drip on the faucet). 7. Recommended extras Lock after inactivity (the AUREN wallet uses 10 minutes). Daily limit and trusted helpers from the Security screen: setSecurity ( Wallet guide ). Plain language. Say "recovery key", "payment" and "fee", not nonce or seed. Error messages from Error codes , translated for your users. Reference implementations Language Code Browser JavaScript website/aurlib.js , website/wallet.js Node.js sdk/js/index.js Python sdk/python/auren.py Both SDKs produce byte-identical signatures; the test suite checks it. Test it Run a local devnet ( node scripts/devnet.js --clean ), take coins from its faucet, and exercise every flow before touching a real network. See the Developer quickstart .

x: Build the apps yourself Downloads are on the releases page . To build them from source: Outputs go to dist/ . Nothing from npm ends up inside the apps. Windows (and Mac, Linux) single-file apps build-exe.js uses Node's single executable support: it copies the node binary on your machine and injects the AUREN program into it. AUREN-Node : double-click for a menu (join the testnet, earn AUR), or run it with arguments like the auren command: AUREN-Node.exe join testnet --earn . AUREN-Wallet : starts the wallet on http://127.0.0.1:8787 and opens your browser. Keys are stored in the browser on your computer. The first run unpacks the program into %LOCALAPPDATA%\AUREN . The files are not code-signed, so Windows SmartScreen may warn. Choose More info, then Run anyway. Needs network access once at build time to fetch the postject injector. Android apps android/build.js uses only the Android SDK command-line tools (aapt2, javac, d8, zipalign, apksigner): no Gradle. It needs the JDK, the Android SDK (platform 34 and build-tools) and Python 3. AUREN Wallet : a WebView around the bundled wallet and explorer, served from http://127.0.0.1:38787 inside the app. Keys stay in the app's storage. AUREN Node : bundles the Node.js runtime for Android (the Termux build, arm64 and x86_64) and runs auren join as a foreground service. Choose the network, turn on Earn, tap Start. It also opens the wallet and explorer served by the node. It needs a 64-bit phone. The node app targets Android API 28 so that the bundled runtime may start from the app's private folder, as Termux does. APKs are signed with a key generated on your machine ( dist/android/auren-release.jks , never committed). Android asks you to allow installs from the source. Android phones cannot reach 127.0.0.1 on your PC. To join a devnet running on your computer, enter its LAN address (for example http://192.168.1.20:9650 ) as the peer.

x: Consensus: Auren BFT-PoS (two-phase, Tendermint-style) Implementation: src/bft.js (pure state machine), wired to the network in src/node.js , primitives in src/consensus.js . Goals Immediate finality; safety while < ⅓ of voting power is Byzantine; stop-rather-than-fork when quorum is unavailable; misbehavior is provable on-chain. Protocol For each height h there are rounds r = 0, 1, 2, … . Voting power is stake-weighted ( min(tokens, cap) ); quorum means strictly more than ⅔ of total power ( power × 3 > total × 2 ), and f+1 means more than ⅓ . Per round: Propose. The proposer for (h, r) (deterministic stake-weighted draw) broadcasts a signed proposal {height, round, polRound, block} . If it holds a valid block from an earlier round (it saw a proof-of-lock for it) it re-proposes that block with polRound set; otherwise it builds a new one. Prevote. On a valid proposal, a validator prevotes the block, unless it is locked on a different block , in which case it prevotes nil. If the proposal carries polRound ≥ 0 , the validator needs to have seen a quorum of prevotes for that block in polRound , and may then prevote it if its lock is at polRound or older (or the same block). No proposal before the timeout, or an invalid one: prevote nil. Precommit. With a proposal and a quorum of prevotes for it in this round, the validator locks on the block ( lockedRound = r ) and precommits it. A quorum of nil prevotes: precommit nil. A quorum of prevotes of any kind starts a prevote timeout, after which it precommits nil. Commit. A quorum of precommits for one block, in any round of the height, finalizes it. The certificate (the precommits) is embedded as lastCommit in the next block, so finality can be verified from the chain alone. Next round. A quorum of precommits of any kind without a decision starts a timeout, then round r+1 . A validator that sees more than ⅓ of voting power in a higher round jumps there immediately. Timeouts grow with the round ( propose = roundTimeoutMs + r·500 ms , votes = roundTimeoutMs/2 + r·500 ms ), which gives the liveness argument below. After a commit, the next height starts one blockTimeMs later. Why it is safe Suppose blocks A and B are both committed at height h . Each has a quorum (> ⅔) of precommits, in rounds rA ≤ rB . If rA = rB the two quorums overlap in more than ⅓ of power, so some validators signed two different precommits in the same round: provable equivocation. If rA < rB , the precommitters of A are locked on A from round rA ; they will prevote nil for any other block unless they see a proof-of-lock for it from a round after rA and before the new proposal, which requires > ⅔ prevotes for B in such a round, and that again forces an overlap of > ⅓ that prevoted for B in violation of their own lock rule, or equivocated. Either way committing two blocks requires ≥ ⅓ of power to break a rule that the protocol punishes. This is the standard Tendermint argument; what we add is the implementation and the tests below. Why it is live (after the network stabilizes) After global stabilization time, message delays are bounded; timeouts grow until they exceed that bound; then a round with an honest proposer in which every honest validator is in the same round finishes. A validator that has seen a proof-of-lock keeps its block as validBlock and re-proposes it, so a block that some validators already locked on is not abandoned. The previous single-phase design could be stuck by two conflicting locks; here a lock can be replaced only by a newer proof-of-lock , so conflicting locks resolve. What a validator persists (before any vote is sent) priv_validator_state.json : for the current height, the votes it signed (keyed by height:round:type ), its lock and valid block. It is written with fsync and an atomic rename before the vote is broadcast. After a crash the node refuses to sign a different vote in a (height, round, type) it already voted in and restores its lock. Keep this file with the node; restoring an old copy while the node was running elsewhere is double signing. Evidence and slashing Two valid signatures from one validator of the same type (prevote or precommit) for the same height and round naming different blocks (nil counts as different) are equivocation evidence. (Votes for different blocks in different rounds are legal after an unlock, so they are not evidence.) Observers queue evidence, the next proposer includes it, and the chain applies it: 5% of bonded stake and of in-flight unbonding burned, validator jailed and tombstoned . Downtime Each block's lastCommit lists signers. A validator missing from more than 50% of a window ( downtimeWindow ) is jailed for jailBlocks and slashed 0.1%; non-signers earn no issuance for that block. Transport Votes and proposals are signed, so forged messages are rejected regardless of transport. They are pushed to every peer ( POST /p2p/msg ) and repaired by pull ( GET /p2p/round-state?height=h , polled while a height is stalled). Blocks and commit certificates are exchanged for catch-up ( /p2p/blocks , /p2p/commit ). Validators are assumed to be directly connected (peer discovery builds a full mesh); relaying across partial topologies is not implemented. How it is tested test/bft.test.js runs real chains, blocks and signatures under a deterministic simulated network and clock (the only simulated parts): the happy path; 5 seeds of 35% message loss with heavy reordering followed by stabilization; a 2/2 partition (no progress, no fork, resumes on healing); a 3/1 partition; crash and restart from the persisted snapshot with no equivocation; an equivocating validator (evidence produced and accepted by the chain, honest 3/4 still finalize); 12 seeds at 50% loss specifically to create the conflicting-lock situations that could halt the old design, each required to recover and never to fork; weighted voting. test/network.test.js runs 4 validators as separate nodes over real HTTP: block production, tx gossip, one node down, halt witho

h: What you need | 1. Generate the genesis (on a trusted machine) | 2. Start the validators | 3. Verify it is one network | 4. Public RPC, wallet and explorer over HTTPS | 5. Faucet | 6. Invite outside validators | 7. Operate it like it matters | What stays your decision
x: Deploying the official public network (CORE TEAM ONLY) For the core team that operates the official seed and validator machines. To simply run a node, see RUN-A-NODE.md . There is only one official testnet and one mainnet; do not create parallel ones. Everything in this repository runs for real on a single machine ( npm run devnet ). A public network additionally needs machines on the internet and a domain, which only you can provide. This guide is the exact path from this repo to a public testnet with a wallet and explorer anyone can open. Mainnet is a different decision with its own gates: see networks/mainnet/README.md . Do not skip them. What you need Item Notes 4+ Linux hosts one validator each, at least 2 cores / 4 GB / SSD; use different providers and regions , otherwise it is one point of failure with four names A domain for TLS RPC + wallet + explorer ( rpc.testnet.<yours> ) and a faucet host Node.js 20+ on each host no other dependencies Time sync chrony /NTP on every host; consensus rounds use local clocks 1. Generate the genesis (on a trusted machine) _private/ contains, per genesis validator, a home directory with its consensus key and config, plus accounts.json (faucet key, operator keys). Treat it as secret : copy each nodeN/ to its own host over SSH, then delete the rest or keep it offline. Commit only genesis.json and network.json . 2. Start the validators On each host (replace the repo path): Open TCP 9650 between the validators (security group allow-list by IP). Use deploy/auren-node.service to keep it running. One instance per consensus key, ever. All nodes must be up within a few minutes of genesisTime (printed by gen:testnet ). 3. Verify it is one network Passes only if all nodes share the genesis hash and agree on a block hash and state root at a common height, finality certificates exist, and no node lags. 4. Public RPC, wallet and explorer over HTTPS Put deploy/Caddyfile in front of one or two nodes (not the validators if you can avoid it: run separate full nodes with --website that peer with them). The node serves the landing page, /wallet.html and /explorer.html itself, and the browser pages automatically use the origin they were loaded from as the RPC URL, so there is nothing else to configure. Block /p2p/* at the proxy (the Caddyfile does). 5. Faucet Put the faucet's URL into networks/networks.json ( testnet.faucet , testnet.rpc , testnet.seeds ) and into the wallet's faucet setting if it is not on the same host name (browser storage key auren.faucet ). The faucet refuses to run on a network whose genesis says mainnet . 6. Invite outside validators Follow docs/validators.md . Give them the genesis file, its hash ( node bin/auren-node.js genesis-hash --home <dir> ), seed URLs, and some testnet AUR (the faucet's 100 AUR is below the 10,000 AUR minimum self-stake, so transfer stake from the treasury key in accounts.json ). 7. Operate it like it matters Monitor /metrics ( deploy/prometheus.yml ) and alert on height stalls and auren_catching_up . Run the fault drills from docs/networks.md and publish results. Back up each validator's priv_validator_key.json and data/priv_validator_state.json . Keep security contact and disclosure policy current ( SECURITY.md ). What stays your decision Hosting, domain, who runs the genesis validators, token distribution, legal review, and when (or whether) to go beyond testnet. The software does not decide these for you.

t: Names, domains and your own TLD
h: How names look | Register a domain | Create your own TLD | Manage a name | Resolve and verify | Transactions
x: Names, domains and your own TLD AUREN has a built-in naming system. You can: Register a domain under .aur ( alice.aur ), or under any TLD someone created ( alice.david ). Create your own TLD ( .david , .mycoin , .shop ) and decide who can register under it and what it costs. Names are optional. The chain works without them. They simply give an address a name people can read. How names look Form Meaning alice Same as alice.aur . alice.aur A name in the built-in .aur namespace. alice.david A name under the user-created .david TLD. Rules: A label is 3 to 63 characters: a-z , 0-9 and hyphens, not starting or ending with a hyphen. A TLD is 3 to 24 characters: a-z and 0-9 , starting with a letter. One level only: a.b.c is not valid. alice.aur and alice.david are different names with different owners. They never collide. Real-world TLDs and country codes ( com , org , eth , btc , uk , io , google , localhost , ...) cannot be created, so nobody can pretend to be a name from another system. Register a domain Wallet: open Wallet → Names , type alice or alice.david , check the price shown, and confirm. CLI: What you pay: Under .aur : the price depends on the name length (shorter costs more). The whole fee is burned . Under a user-created TLD: the TLD owner's yearly price times the number of years. The owner receives their configured share and the rest is burned . The TLD owner registers names under their own TLD for free (only the normal network fee applies). Create your own TLD Wallet: open Wallet → Names → Create your own TLD . Choose: Setting Meaning TLD The name, for example david for .david . Open If on, anyone can register names under it. If off, only you can. Price Yearly price per name, in AUR. 0 means free. Your share The percentage of each registration paid to you (up to 90%). The rest is burned. CLI: Creating a TLD costs the network parameter tld.price (burned). It is set per network and can change by governance. You can change the price, the share and whether it is open at any time. Names that are already registered keep working. Manage a name Every name has an owner, a target address, and optional records. Transferring a name resets its target and records, so a buyer never inherits the old owner's settings. Resolve and verify Anyone can look up a name without trusting a server. The node returns a Merkle proof, and the light client in website/anr.js checks it against the validator set pinned at genesis. A proof for bob.david cannot be passed off as bob.aur . JSON-RPC: aur_resolve , aur_resolveDomain , aur_getTlds , aur_getTld . See rpc-api.md . The explorer lists all TLDs under Names . Transactions Type Body registerTld tld , open , price , ownerShareBps setTldPolicy tld , open , price , ownerShareBps (owner only) transferTld tld , newOwner (owner only) registerDomain name ( label or label.tld ), years Registrations under a user-created TLD pay the TLD owner, so they use a block-wide lane (they run one after another). .aur registrations still run in parallel. See also name-resolution.md for the proof format and the cross-system resolver.

x: EVM layer AUREN runs Ethereum bytecode. Contracts deploy and run on the same validators, fee market and state as everything else, and Ethereum tools connect through standard JSON-RPC. Code: src/evm/ (interpreter vm.js , journaled state state.js , chain glue host.js , raw-transaction parser ethtx.js , RPC rpc.js , Keccak/RLP/secp256k1). Tests: test/evm.test.js , test/evm-chain.test.js , differential harness scripts/evm-diff.js . Connecting a wallet or tool devnet testnet mainnet RPC URL http://127.0.0.1:9650 your node not launched Chain ID 77001 77002 77000 Currency AUR, 18 decimals AUR AUR (Check chainlist.org for conflicts before any public launch; these numbers are placeholders.) To get test funds, ask the faucet for the account's AUREN address , which for an Ethereum key is bech32("daur", [4, ...20-byte Ethereum address]) (helper: keyFromHex(addrHex, 4, 'daur') in src/evm/host.js ). Verified live: with unmodified ethers v6 against a running 4-validator devnet: connect, eth_chainId , fee data, deploy a contract (gas 77,708), getCode , eth_call , getStorageAt , send 2.5 AUR, nonces, balances, block with transactions. MetaMask itself has not been tested (no browser wallet automation here); it uses the same RPC methods, so it should work, but treat that as unconfirmed. From the command line Gas is estimated automatically ( --gas N to override; --simulate for a dry run). The block explorer shows gas, return data, logs and created contracts on each transaction page, and accepts Ethereum transaction hashes in search. What is implemented Opcodes and rules: Ethereum "Shanghai" : all opcodes through PUSH0, EIP-2929 warm/cold access, EIP-2200/3529 SSTORE and refunds, EIP-3541, EIP-3651, EIP-3855, EIP-3860, CREATE/CREATE2, depth and code-size limits, static calls, SELFDESTRUCT (Shanghai semantics). Precompiles 1-5 and 9 : ecrecover, SHA-256, RIPEMD-160, identity, modexp (EIP-2565), blake2f. Precompiles 6-8 (bn254 add/mul/pairing) are NOT implemented : calls fail and burn the forwarded gas. Contracts that verify Groth16/zk-SNARK proofs will not work yet. Not in Shanghai (not implemented): transient storage (TLOAD/TSTORE), MCOPY, blob opcodes (Cancun). Transactions: (a) native evm transactions signed with any AUREN key (Ed25519 or passkey); (b) raw Ethereum transactions (legacy EIP-155, EIP-2930/EIP-1559 type 1-2 without access lists) signed with secp256k1, accepted through eth_sendRawTransaction . The raw bytes are the signature: the chain recomputes the transaction envelope from them and rejects any mismatch, so no field can be altered. RPC: eth_chainId, eth_blockNumber, eth_getBalance, eth_getTransactionCount, eth_gasPrice, eth_maxPriorityFeePerGas, eth_feeHistory, eth_getCode, eth_getStorageAt, eth_call, eth_estimateGas, eth_sendRawTransaction, eth_getTransactionReceipt, eth_getTransactionByHash, eth_getBlockByNumber/Hash, eth_getLogs , net_* , web3_clientVersion . Not implemented: eth_subscribe /filters, debug_* / trace_* , eth_getProof , access lists. POST / and POST /rpc both work. How it fits the chain Addresses. An account's EVM address is the 20-byte hash inside its bech32 address. Ethereum keys use address scheme 4 ( keccak256(pubkey)[12:] , so the EVM address equals the Ethereum address); contracts use scheme 3. Mapping is stored in eaddr ; contract code in ecode ; storage in estor (all in the Merkle state root). Units. 1 AUR = 1e9 sparks = 1e18 wei : contracts see 18-decimal values. The chain's smallest unit is 1 spark, so value transfers must be multiples of 1e9 wei; a call that sends a fractional amount fails (a raw transaction with such a value is rejected at submission). Fees. EVM gas is the compute dimension; a transaction also reserves ceil(gasLimit/1000) state units, so the effective gas price is baseFee.compute + baseFee.state/1000 sparks per gas ( eth_gasPrice quotes this plus rounding). Unused gas is refunded; the base part is burned, the tip goes to the proposer. A reverted call still pays for the gas it used and does not move value or change state. Security features apply. The account daily limit also caps value sent by EVM transactions. Execution is sequential. EVM transactions declare a wildcard access set, so a block that contains one runs in block order (no parallel lanes). Block context. COINBASE = proposer, TIMESTAMP = block time (s), NUMBER , GASLIMIT = compute limit, BASEFEE = per-gas price in wei, PREVRANDAO = 0 (no randomness beacon yet: do not build lotteries on it), BLOCKHASH for the last 256 blocks, CHAINID = the EVM chain id. How it was verified Differential testing against the reference EVM ( @ethereumjs/evm , Shanghai): 7,569 programs (hand-written plus a stack-aware fuzzer with several seeds, including nested CALL/CREATE/DELEGATECALL/STATICCALL, SELFDESTRUCT, logs, memory growth, SSTORE refunds and precompiles) produced zero differences in success, gas, return data, logs, storage, balances and refunds. 260 of them are recorded in test/fixtures/evm-golden.json and replayed by npm test without any external dependency. Keccak-256, RLP and secp256k1 recovery cross-checked against ethers on random inputs; ethers-signed transactions parse and execute ( test/evm-chain.test.js ). Chain behaviour tested: deploy/call/send via raw Ethereum transactions and native transactions, gas refunds, reverts, daily-limit enforcement, replay protection, tamper detection, deterministic replay on a second node, token conservation. Known limitations Not audited. The interpreter is verified against one reference implementation, not against the official Ethereum test suite ( ethereum/tests ), and not formally. Precompiles 6-8 missing (above); Cancun opcodes missing. The fee model approximates Ethereum's: gas costs are Ethereum's, but its price comes from two dimensions, so eth_estimateGas returns gasUsed × 1.2 and wallets' fee estimates are slightly conservative. An account funded under one address scheme but used from another needs the right AUREN address when receiving from the fauc

x: FAQ The basics What is AUREN? A public network with its own coin, AUR. You can send it, stake it, give your wallet a name, and run apps on it. What is AUR? The coin of AUREN. 1 AUR is split into 1,000,000,000 tiny parts called sparks. Is mainnet live? Not yet. It launches after independent security audits and a long public test. Today the devnet and testnet are live. What is the difference between devnet, testnet and mainnet? Mainnet is the real network. The testnet is the official place to try everything before launch. The devnet is for early features and may be reset. There is exactly one of each; you join them rather than create them. See Networks . Money How much does a payment cost? A tiny fraction of a cent. At the minimum fee level a transfer costs 0.000026 AUR. Fees rise a little only when the network is busy. Where does the fee go? It is burned: removed from the supply forever. Nobody collects it. That makes AUR slightly scarcer over time. How do I get AUR on the testnet or devnet? Open Receive in the wallet and press Get 1,000 AUR . What is staking and is it safe? Staking locks your AUR behind a validator to earn rewards. See the Staking guide for the risks. Where do rewards come from? Newly issued AUR. See Tokenomics . Wallet and safety I forgot my password. Add your wallet again using your recovery key ( I already have a wallet ) and choose a new password. Without the recovery key nobody can recover it, including us. Where is my wallet stored? On your device only, locked with your password. Can AUREN staff recover my coins? No. Nobody can. Can I use my Ethereum wallet? Yes. AUREN speaks the Ethereum protocol, so tools like MetaMask can connect with the chain ID from Integrate . Names What is alice.aur ? An easy name for your address. Register it in the wallet's Names tab. What is a TLD? The ending of a name, like .aur or .david . You can create your own ending and set its price. See domains . Can I register alice.com ? No. Real-world endings like .com and .eth are reserved so nobody can imitate them. Nodes Do I earn anything by running a node? Yes. Start your node with Earn turned on. It locks a deposit, proves each epoch that it stores the chain and shares a pool of new AUR. See Node rewards . Will it use a lot of space or data? Very little on the test networks. A phone should stay plugged in. Can I run a node on my phone? Yes, with the AUREN Node app for 64-bit Android. For developers Is there an API? Yes: REST and JSON-RPC on every node, plus Ethereum-compatible JSON-RPC. See Integrate and the Developer quickstart . Are there SDKs? JavaScript and Python, with no dependencies. See Integrate .

h: What it is | Resources | Base fee update | Paying | Lanes (parallel execution) | Spam resistance | Known gaps
x: Adaptive Execution Market What it is A fee mechanism that (1) prices two resources separately, (2) gives each transaction type a fixed, quotable cost, and (3) schedules transactions with disjoint state access into independent lanes. It combines established ideas: EIP-1559 base-fee dynamics, multi-dimensional resource pricing, and declared-access-set scheduling. It is not claimed to be novel as a whole; it is claimed to be specified precisely and tested. Resources dimension meaning default block limit target (50%) compute execution work in abstract units 30,000,000 15,000,000 state bytes of state written (approximate) 200,000 100,000 At default limits a block can hold ≈ 1,428 plain transfers by compute (the binding dimension), i.e. a protocol cap of roughly 700 transfers/s at 2 s blocks. Limits are parameters and should be set from testnet measurements, not marketing. Base fee update Per dimension, from the parent block's usage: So a full block raises each base fee by 12.5% (e.g. 40 → 45), an empty block lowers it by 12.5%, and a block exactly at target leaves it unchanged. Default start {compute: 4, state: 200} sparks/unit; floor {1, 50} . A transfer therefore costs 21,000×4 + 100×200 = 104,000 sparks ≈ 0.000104 AUR at the start and 21,000×1 + 100×50 = 26,000 sparks = 0.000026 AUR at the floor. That is cents-or-less at any plausible price, and the fee is burned, not paid to anyone. Paying baseCost = cost.compute × base.compute + cost.state × base.state is burned . The sender signs maxFee and tip . Wallets quote aur_feeQuote , set maxFee = baseCost × 2 + tip to absorb two blocks of worst-case increases (1.125² ≈ 1.27), and are refunded implicitly: only baseCost + min(tip, maxFee − baseCost) is charged. Because costs are fixed per type, there is no gas estimation and no out-of-gas failure. The trade-off: no user-deployed code yet. When an EVM layer arrives (Phase 2) it will meter compute and state through these same two dimensions. Lanes (parallel execution) Every transaction type declares an access set , the keys it may read or write, e.g. a transfer touches acct:<from> and acct:<to> . scheduleLanes runs union-find over the keys: Transactions sharing any key end up in the same lane, in block order. Others are in different lanes and may execute in any order, or on separate threads. Shared hotspots would defeat this, so they are removed by construction: fees, burns and tips accumulate during the block and are applied once at the end; the proposer's balance is not touched mid-block. Guarantee (tested): for a random mix of 60 transfers, delegations and name registrations, executing lanes in forward, reverse and shuffled order yields identical state roots. If you add a transaction type whose handler touches a key not in its access set, this guarantee silently breaks. Add it to access and extend the test. The reference node executes lanes sequentially on one thread (about 9,400 transfers/s validating, see npm run bench ). The scheduler is the foundation for threaded or multi-process execution; it is not yet exploited for speed. Spam resistance Every transaction pays at least the floor base fee, so spam has a price. Sustained congestion drives the base fee up exponentially (+12.5%/block ≈ ×3.2 in 10 blocks), which is what throttles it. Per-sender nonce gaps are limited (256) and mempool size is capped (20,000); replacing a pending transaction requires ≥ 10% higher tip. State-heavy abuse is priced on its own state dimension rather than hiding in compute. Known gaps Cost constants are initial estimates, not benchmark-derived. They must be recalibrated on a distributed testnet. Tips are a simple first-price auction for the proposer; priority ordering is not yet MEV-resistant. No per-account or per-contract hotspot pricing yet (a contract everyone touches serializes execution); this is a research item for Phase 2.

h: What governance can change | Lifecycle | Properties | Using it | Limitations (honest)
x: On-chain governance Implementation: src/gov.js (rules), src/tx.js ( submitProposal , vote ), src/chain.js (settlement, live parameters). Tests: test/gov.test.js . What governance can change Only the whitelisted parameters below, each with a hard range enforced both when a proposal is submitted and again when it executes. Everything else (block time, address prefix, token decimals, signature schemes, the governance rules themselves) needs a new network or a coordinated software upgrade. Parameter Range limits.compute , limits.state 1e6..1e9, 1e4..1e7 (block resource limits) baseFeeChangeDenominator 2..64 minBaseFee.compute , minBaseFee.state 1..1,000,000 sparks maxValidators 4..300 maxVotingPowerBps 100..10000 maxCommissionBps 0..5000 issuance.decayBps , issuance.floorPpm 0..5000, 0..50000 (the floor can never exceed 5%/yr) slashing.doubleSignBps , slashing.downtimeBps 0..5000, 0..1000 domain.price3/4/5 0..10^15 sparks The initial issuance rate, the unbonding period and the governance parameters are deliberately not changeable. Lifecycle Submit ( submitProposal {title, description, changes} ): 1-5 parameter changes. A deposit (mainnet default 1,000 AUR) is escrowed and counted in the supply invariant. Vote for votingBlocks (mainnet 201,600 ≈ 7 days): yes , no , abstain , veto . Weight is the voter's bonded stake (sum of all their delegations, evaluated at tally time). Validators do not vote on behalf of their delegators. Re-voting replaces the earlier vote. Accounts without stake can vote but carry no weight. Tally at the end of the period: no quorum (voted stake < 33.4% of all bonded stake) → rejected, deposit burned veto ≥ 33.4% of voted stake → rejected, deposit burned otherwise yes / (yes + no + veto) > 50% passes; the deposit is refunded whether it passes or fails the threshold. abstain counts toward quorum only. Timelock ( timelockBlocks , mainnet 86,400 ≈ 2 days): a passed proposal waits before it takes effect, so users can exit, validators can prepare, and the community can react. Execute at the end of block E : the changes are re-validated and stored as overrides in state; the new parameters apply from block E+1 on every node, deterministically (replay-tested). Properties Deterministic and replayable: overrides live in state ( meta/params ), so a node replaying the log reaches identical parameters and an identical state root. Live proof: on a real 4-validator devnet, a proposal raised limits.compute from 30,000,000 to 45,000,000 after a 3/4 stake vote and a timelock (voting 60 blocks, timelock 20 blocks on devnet). Conservation: deposits are escrowed supply; burn/refund paths are tested against the invariant. Parallel-safe: submitProposal and vote share the global:gov access key, so a vote never races the creation of its proposal under lane scheduling. Using it The web wallet has a Govern tab (proposals, live tally bars, vote buttons, submit form). REST: GET /proposals ; JSON-RPC: aur_getProposals . Limitations (honest) Plutocratic by design. Weight is stake. There is no delegation of votes, quadratic weighting or identity layer. Large holders dominate; the veto and quorum rules and the timelock are the checks. No "validators vote for delegators who abstain" inheritance (as in some chains). Delegators must vote themselves, which lowers turnout but avoids validator overreach. Not an upgrade mechanism. It changes parameters only. Changing consensus rules or transaction formats still needs a coordinated software release, with a height agreed in advance. No emergency path and no protection against a hostile supermajority beyond the timelock; a malicious majority could, for example, set issuance.floorPpm to 5% (the cap) or raise name prices to the range maximum. The ranges above are what bound that. Parameter-range choices are initial and should be reviewed before mainnet.

h: What is supported | Things to know | Ledger and Trezor | Testing, and what is not covered
x: Hardware keys and passkeys What is supported Signature scheme 2: WebAuthn / ECDSA P-256. The web wallet can create a key inside a security key (YubiKey and similar FIDO2 keys), a platform authenticator (Touch ID, Windows Hello, Android biometrics) or a phone passkey. The private key never leaves the device and every transaction requires the user's touch or biometric. How it works on-chain ( src/crypto.js verifyWebAuthn , src/tx.js ): Address = bech32(scheme byte 2 ‖ sha256(2 ‖ publicKey)[0:20]) ; the public key is the uncompressed P-256 point (65 bytes). A transaction carries scheme: 2 , that pub , and sig = {authData, clientData, signature} . The wallet asks the device to sign the challenge sha256(signingBytes(tx)) . The chain checks: clientData.type == "webauthn.get" ; clientData.challenge == base64url(sha256(signingBytes(tx))) (so a signature is bound to the exact transaction, chain ID and nonce, and cannot be transplanted); the user-present flag is set; and the ECDSA signature over authData ‖ sha256(clientData) verifies under the account's key. Recovery can move any account onto a hardware key: guardians approve recoveryApprove {account, newPub, newScheme: 2} . Things to know Not exportable, so use guardians. A hardware key cannot be backed up. Losing the device loses the key; set guardians (Security tab) so the account can be recovered to a new key. Bound to the site name. WebAuthn credentials are scoped to the host name (relying-party ID) of the page that created them ( localhost , wallet.example.org ). They cannot be used from another host name, which is also what stops a phishing site from asking your key to sign. HTTPS or localhost only. Browsers expose WebAuthn only in secure contexts. Signature size: about 200-300 bytes more than Ed25519 per transaction (authenticator data + client data). Fine at current block limits; this is a measured trade-off, not free. Approval prompt shows less than the review screen. The device usually shows only "sign in to <site>". The wallet's review dialog (with the node's dry-run) is the place where you check amounts and recipients, then the touch confirms. Ledger and Trezor Not supported yet, and this is a hard external dependency, not a missing feature flag. A Ledger signs only through an app installed on the device, and no AUREN app exists. Building one means writing and submitting device firmware (C, Ledger SDK) and passing Ledger's review; it cannot be verified without a physical device. WebAuthn gives the same property (key never leaves hardware, user confirmation per transaction) with devices people already own. A Ledger app is on the roadmap for after the transaction format is frozen. Testing, and what is not covered test/webauthn.test.js verifies the chain-side logic with real P-256 cryptography and the exact byte formats a browser returns, via a software authenticator: acceptance and execution, rejection when the amount, nonce or chain ID changes, rejection of a signature transplanted from another transaction, rejection without user presence, parity of address derivation between the browser library and the node, and guardian recovery onto a hardware key (old key stops working). Not covered by automated tests: a physical security key or biometric prompt (a test runner cannot touch a YubiKey), and browser-specific differences. Manual checklist before relying on it: Open the wallet on http://localhost:<port> or HTTPS in current Chrome/Edge/Safari/Firefox. "Hardware key / passkey" → create; the device prompts; the wallet shows an address. Fund it from the faucet; send a transaction; the device prompts; the transaction confirms. Set a guardian, and complete a recovery to another key. Repeat with a second authenticator type (platform vs. USB key).

Add the network with the chain ID from the table. The full, machine-readable reference is the OpenAPI file . Browse the methods in rpc-api.md . SDKs Language Where Notes JavaScript (Node 20+) sdk/js Client , Wallet , amounts in AUR JavaScript (browser) website/aurlib.js the library the wallet uses; global Aur Python 3 sdk/python/auren.py no dependencies, pure-Python Ed25519 Any language this page sign a transaction yourself, below JavaScript: Python: Keys and addresses Scheme byte Key Use 0 Ed25519 software wallets (the default) 2 ECDSA P-256 (WebAuthn) phone passkeys and security keys 4 secp256k1 (Ethereum) Ethereum wallets; the address is the same 20 bytes as 0x… An address is Bech32 of [scheme byte] + sha256(scheme byte ‖ public key)[0..20] with the network prefix. Ethereum accounts also answer at their 0x address ( GET /account/0x… ). One seed can serve every network; only the prefix changes. Sign a transaction yourself A transaction is a JSON object: Nonce: use pendingNonce from aur_getAccount . Fee: maxFee must be at least the base fee for the type (from aur_feeQuote ) plus your tip . Setting it to twice the quote is safe; unused fee is not charged. The fee is burned. Sign: build the object without sig , serialize it as canonical JSON (keys sorted, no spaces, amounts as decimal strings), prepend the bytes AUREN/tx/v1 followed by a zero byte, and sign those bytes with your key. Put the signature (hex) in sig . Check: send it to aur_simulate first. It returns the effects, the fee and whether it would succeed, without changing anything. Send: aur_sendTx . The result has the transaction hash ( sha256 of the canonical JSON including sig ). Wait: poll aur_getTx(hash) until status is confirmed ; receipt.status is 1 on success. Transaction types and their bodies are listed in protocol.md . The common ones: Type Body transfer to , amount delegate / undelegate validator , amount claim validator registerDomain name ( alice , alice.aur or alice.david ), years setDomainTarget name , target registerTld tld , open , price , ownerShareBps registerNode / nodeProof see node-rewards.md evm smart-contract calls; use the Ethereum RPC instead Reference implementations to copy: signTx in src/tx.js (JavaScript) and Wallet.build in sdk/python/auren.py . The two produce byte-identical signatures, which a test checks. Names Look up: GET /domain/{name} or aur_resolve (with a Merkle proof). website/anr.js verifies proofs on the client, so a wallet does not have to trust the node. Show a name for an address: aur_reverse , checked in both directions. Register .aur names and your own name endings with registerDomain and registerTld ; see domains.md . The website's Names page links straight into the wallet, so you can send users there: wallet.html?tab=names&name=alice.aur . Smart contracts and Ethereum tools Point any Ethereum tool at http://NODE:9650/rpc with the Ethereum chain ID above. Raw Ethereum transactions are accepted. See evm.md . Tips for wallet makers Use aur_simulate before every send and show the user the fee and result. Show amounts in AUR, never sparks. Round only for display. Refuse to pay a name that resolves differently in two places (the ambiguous result of aur_resolve across namespaces). Run or choose your own node for production, and pin the genesis hash. Never log seeds. Keep them encrypted at rest.

h: A. Public testnet (do this first; ~1 hour of work) | B. Mainnet (real value): gates, not shortcuts | What each piece is and where it lives | Honest limits
x: Launching a network: the complete path (CORE TEAM ONLY) Not for users or node operators. There is exactly one mainnet, one testnet and one devnet, and they are created once, by the core team, using the tools below. If you just want to use AUREN or run a node, read GETTING-STARTED.md and RUN-A-NODE.md and join the existing network with ./auren join testnet . Running make-bundles yourself creates a different, unofficial network that no wallet or explorer will recognize. Everything below is implemented in this repository and was exercised on a real multi-process network. The parts that need your servers, domain, people and legal decisions are marked YOU . A. Public testnet (do this first; ~1 hour of work) YOU: get 4+ machines (different providers/regions; 2 cores, 4 GB, SSD) with public IPs. Install Node.js 20+. Put the repo on each machine ( git clone , or copy the folder). On one trusted machine generate the bundles (keys are created here, treat the output as secret): `` bash node scripts/make-bundles.js --network testnet --hosts 203.0.113.10,203.0.113.11,203.0.113.12,203.0.113.13 --out ./bundles ` It prints the genesis hash and genesis time. Each bundles/nodeN/ holds that validator's genesis, key, config (peers already pointing at the other hosts), start.sh , start.ps1` and a systemd unit. YOU: copy bundles/nodeN/ to machine N over SSH. h: The problem | The six failure modes and what ANR-1 does | Identifiers | On-chain objects (all in the state root, so all provable) | Verified resolution protocol | Resolver policy (what wallets MUST do) | Testing | What ANR-1 does not do
x: ANR-1: AUREN Name Resolution (fixing name-service fragmentation) The problem Independently built name systems do not share a common way to identify , resolve and trust names. The same string ( alice.david ) can exist in several systems with different owners; wallets support some systems and not others; ordinary browsers and DNS know nothing about them; look-alike names enable phishing; a wrong resolver answer sends real money to the wrong place. Ownership (a chain, a contract) is separate from resolution (registries, resolvers) and from use (wallets, apps), and nothing connects the three layers. A single central resolver does not fix this: you still have to decide whose answer to trust, who writes the rules, and how a wallet checks the answer . ANR-1 is a set of rules plus working code for exactly those three questions. It does not claim to unify every name system; it makes the failures visible and safe. The six failure modes and what ANR-1 does # Problem ANR-1 answer Where ① Namespace collision : same name, different owners A name is only fully identified together with its namespace : alice.aur@auren-mainnet-1 (chain ID = namespace). The resolver asks every namespace it knows; if namespaces disagree it returns ambiguous and offers no address. Machine interfaces must carry the namespace. website/anr.js UniversalResolver ; aur_resolve returns chainId + genesisHash ② Resolver incompatibility One interface, pluggable adapters, one result type: {status, candidates[{source, namespace, address, verified}], sendable, notes} . Adapters: AUREN (native), ENS, DNS. website/anr.js ③ Wallet integration fragmentation The wallet calls resolve(input) once; adapters live behind it. A new name system = a new adapter, not a new wallet feature. The explorer uses the same library. wallet.js , explorer.js use ANR ④ Gap to the ordinary internet DNS bridge: a domain publishes _auren.example.com TXT "v=ANR1 aur:auren-mainnet-1=aur1…" . Resolved over DNS-over-HTTPS; DNSSEC-validated answers are marked, unsigned ones are not. ENS names resolve through the Ethereum JSON-RPC (registry → resolver → addr ). dnsResolve , ensResolve ⑤ Trust and security (a) Verified resolution: AUREN answers come with Merkle proofs and a commit certificate and are checked by a light client ; a lying node is downgraded to unverified . (b) Registry hygiene: ASCII only (no homograph alphabets), no -- (blocks xn-- spoofing), a name may not look like an address or key. (c) Reverse names are forward-verified : address → name is shown only if the name still resolves back to that address, so nobody can claim a name they do not hold. (d) Safe transfers: selling a name resets its target and records, so the buyer's funds can never be routed to the seller. (e) Wallet policy: ambiguous or missing → refuse; unverified → explicit confirmation; the review dialog shows name, namespace, and how it was verified. chain: src/tx.js , src/chain.js ; client: anr.js , wallet.js ⑥ Ecosystem lock-in Everything is open: the proof format, the library, the DNS record format. Ownership and resolution live on the same chain, and the proof lets anyone verify without using the operator's infrastructure. Records are multi-chain : one name holds addr:<namespace>:<ref> entries (Ethereum, Bitcoin, …) so a name is not tied to one chain's tooling. setRecord , aur_resolve Identifiers On-chain objects (all in the state root, so all provable) dom/<name> → {owner, target, expiresAt, records?} (≤ 16 records, values ≤ 256 printable chars). rev/<address> → {name} , only trusted when dom/<name>.target == address and the name is live. Transactions: registerDomain , setDomainTarget , transferDomain (resets target + records), setRecord , setPrimary (accepted only if the name already points to you). Verified resolution protocol aur_resolve(name) returns the record and a proof bundle: The client ( ANR.verifyResolution ) checks, without trusting the node: sha256(canon(header)) == block.hash . Both Merkle paths fold to header.stateRoot . The response matches the proven record, and the name had not expired at that height. More than ⅔ of the proven validator set signed the block (Ed25519 verification of each precommit). More than ⅓ of the validator set the client already trusts also signed it. This is the light-client rule: it stops an attacker from presenting a complete, self-consistent fake history signed by their own validators. (Tested: a fully forged chain is rejected.) Trust anchor. The client's initial trusted set is computed from the genesis file , whose hash is checked against a pinned genesis hash ( networks/networks.json , shipped with the app). After each verified proof the trusted set advances to the proven one and is stored, so it follows validator-set changes. If the node's genesis hash is not pinned (a custom network) results are still verified relative to that node's genesis, and the UI says "genesis not pinned". Limits (honest): Trusting period: if the trusted set is so old that fewer than ⅓ of it still signs (long absence), verification fails closed ("re-sync"), because sequential header sync is not implemented yet. Freshness: a proof is for the latest block the node had; a malicious node can serve an older (still valid) block. The proof carries the block time and height so the wallet can show it. Expiry/transfer in the last few blocks could be missed. Non-membership: "name not registered" is not proven; a node can falsely say a name does not exist (it cannot make a different address verify). Pre-registered key reuse: a name resolves to what its owner wrote; verification proves authenticity of the record , not that the owner is who you believe. Check the name carefully. t: Node rewards: earn AUR by running a node
h: How you earn | Run an earning node | Rules | Check on it | Manual control (CLI) | Transactions | What this is not
x: Node rewards: earn AUR by running a node Anyone who runs a full node can earn AUR. You do not need to be a validator. How you earn Bond. Your node locks a bond (a deposit) once. You get it back when you stop (after the unbonding period). Prove. Once per epoch the network picks one old block at random. Your node proves it still has that block's data. Only a node that really stores the chain can do this, and the proof is tied to your node's address, so it cannot be copied from another node. Get paid. Each block, a share of newly issued AUR goes into a node reward pool . At the end of every epoch the pool is split equally between all nodes that proved they store the chain, and paid to each node's payout address. If nobody proves, the pool rolls over to the next epoch. All of this is done by the node software for you. Run an earning node On the devnet and testnet the node asks the faucet for coins to cover the bond. Otherwise, send the bond (plus a little for fees) to the address the node prints when it starts. The node then registers itself and proves storage every epoch. Leave it running. devnet testnet mainnet Bond 100 AUR 500 AUR 10,000 AUR (default) Epoch 120 blocks 1,800 blocks 14,400 blocks (default) Pool share 10% of issuance 10% 10% What 10% means: it is 10% of the newly issued AUR, not of anyone's balance. With issuance at 3% a year, that is 0.3% of supply a year, shared between the nodes. Nobody pays it: it replaces part of what validators would have received. Fees are separate and tiny (about 0.000026 AUR for a transfer at the floor), and they are burned. The pool share comes out of the normal issuance. Validator rewards are issuance minus the pool share, so total issuance does not change. Rules You must be bonded before an epoch starts to earn in it. A new node starts earning from the next epoch. Epoch 0 has no history to challenge, so earning starts in epoch 1. One proof per node per epoch. A node that is offline or does not store the chain earns nothing that epoch. It loses nothing else. Running many identities does not help: each one needs its own bond and gets one equal share, the same return as one honest node per bond. Check on it Returns the pool, current epoch, the challenged block, and every registered node with whether it has proved this epoch. The explorer shows the same under Nodes . JSON-RPC: aur_getNodes . Manual control (CLI) Transactions Type Body registerNode payout unregisterNode nodeProof epoch , digest = sha256( address + | + canonical JSON of the challenged block's header and txs) Parameters: node.bond , node.epochBlocks , node.poolBps . See src/noderew.js . What this is not Rewards go to nodes that store the chain, not to nodes that merely exist. Serving data to others and uptime beyond one proof per epoch are not measured. Validators still earn the largest share, for proposing and signing blocks.

x: Protocol specification (v0.1) Normative description of what src/ implements. Where the code and this document disagree, that is a bug in one of them. Encoding Canonical JSON ( canon ): object keys sorted, BigInt rendered as decimal strings, undefined omitted. All hashes and signatures are over canonical JSON. Hash: SHA-256, hex. Merkle root: binary tree over 32-byte leaves, odd node promoted; empty list = sha256("") . Signatures: Ed25519. Domain tags: AUREN/tx/v1\0 , AUREN/vote/v1\0 , AUREN/block/v1\0 , AUREN/gentx/v1\0 . Units: 1 AUR = 10⁹ sparks. All amounts are decimal strings on the wire, BigInt in state. Addresses Bech32 (BIP-173). Payload is 21 bytes: scheme (0 = Ed25519, 1 = reserved ML-DSA, 2 = WebAuthn ECDSA P-256: see hardware-wallets.md ) ‖ sha256(scheme ‖ pubkey)[0:20] . Human-readable prefix per network: aur (mainnet), taur (testnet), daur (devnet). Transactions chainId is inside the signed bytes: no cross-network replay. Valid if: signature verifies, from is the address of pub (or, after recovery, pub equals the account's authPub ), nonce equals the account nonce, maxFee ≥ baseCost , and spendable balance ≥ baseCost + tip . Fee: baseCost = cost.compute × baseFee.compute + cost.state × baseFee.state (burned). tip = min(tx.tip, maxFee − baseCost) (to the proposer at end of block). A transaction failing these checks makes the block invalid. A transaction failing in its handler is included with status: 0 ; fee and nonce are consumed, effects reverted. Types and fixed resource costs type compute state body transfer 21,000 100 to , amount delegate 60,000 250 validator , amount undelegate 70,000 300 validator , amount claim 40,000 100 validator createValidator 150,000 600 consPub , commissionBps , moniker , amount unjail 40,000 100 registerDomain 80,000 400 name ( label or label.tld ), years registerNode 60,000 300 payout (see node-rewards.md ) unregisterNode 50,000 250 nodeProof 60,000 150 epoch , digest registerTld 100,000 500 tld , open , price , ownerShareBps (see domains.md ) setTldPolicy 50,000 200 tld , open , price , ownerShareBps transferTld 40,000 100 tld , newOwner setDomainTarget 40,000 100 name , target transferDomain 40,000 100 name , newOwner (resets target and records) setRecord 50,000 300 name , key ( addr:<ns>:<ref> / text:<k> / content ), value | null setPrimary 40,000 100 name | null (only if the name already points to you) submitProposal 200,000 1,000 title , description , changes{param: value} (see governance.md ) vote 50,000 150 id , option ( yes / no / abstain / veto ) setSecurity 60,000 400 guardians[] , threshold , delayBlocks , dailyLimit | null securityCancel 40,000 100 account recoveryApprove 50,000 200 account , newPub recoveryCancel 40,000 100 Each type also declares an access set (keys it may read/write); see fee-market.md . Block A block is valid iff: height/parent/chain match; time increases (and is not > local clock + 5 s when proposed); the proposer equals the deterministic draw for (height, round) ; sig is valid; baseFee equals the value derived from the parent; lastCommit is a valid >⅔ certificate for the parent (height ≥ 2); all roots recompute; usage is within limits; and re-execution yields the committed stateRoot and receiptsRoot . Block execution order Evidence : equivocation proofs (two votes of one type, same height and round, different blocks) slash, jail and tombstone. See consensus.md . Liveness : count validators missing from lastCommit ; at window boundaries jail those that missed > maxMissedBps . Transactions in lane order (conflicting transactions keep block order). Fees accumulate; they are not credited mid-block. End of block : credit tips to the proposer; mature unbonding entries; execute due recoveries; mint issuance to the previous block's signers (reward-index accounting); update supply and burned ; recompute the active set for the next height. State Namespaces: acct (balance, nonce, authPub, vesting, security), val , del , unb , dom , rec , meta (supply, burned, activeSet, lastValset). stateRoot is the merkle root over sorted (namespace, key, canon(value)) leaves. Invariant (tested): supply = Σ balances + Σ bonded tokens + Σ unbonding + Σ accrued-unclaimed rewards . Staking Delegations hold shares of a validator's pool, so slashing reduces everyone proportionally. Rewards use a per-validator reward index ( index += reward × 10¹⁸ / totalShares ); settled lazily on delegate/undelegate/claim. Commission is accrued separately. Unbonding takes unbondingBlocks (mainnet default 1,209,600 ≈ 28 days). Unbonding stake remains slashable for infractions committed before it began. Active set: top maxValidators by bonded tokens among non-jailed validators with ≥ minSelfStake ; power = min(tokens, cap) . Parameters Defaults live in src/params.js ; a genesis file may override any of them. Get AUREN Download the package from the official site's Run a node page ( /run-a-node.html ) and unpack it. It is under 200 KB and contains no keys. Every node started with --website serves it at /downloads/ . 2. Join Windows (easiest): unzip, right-click install\windows\Install-AUREN.ps1 → Run with PowerShell (installs Node.js if missing, adds AUREN Node to the Start Menu, can start it at sign-in), then open AUREN Node . Or in a terminal: auren.cmd join testnet . macOS / Linux: install Node.js 20+ from nodejs.org, then in the unpacked folder: Android: install Termux (F-Droid), copy the package in, then sh install/android/termux-setup.sh . This runs a real node inside Termux. There is no standalone Android app yet: an APK needs the Android SDK and a signing key, which this project does not ship. The first run creates ~/.auren/testnet (Windows: C:\Users\<you>\.auren\testnet ) and syncs from the network's seed nodes. Leave the window open. 3. Check it Your node also serves the website, wallet and explorer: open the address printed in the node window (default port 9650). Options Option Meaning --peers http://host:port,… nodes to connect to (default: the published seed nodes; if none are published yet, you must give at least one) --port 9650 port for your node --home <dir> where data lives (never share one folder between two networks) --public accept connections from other machines (default: only this computer) --tls-cert f --tls-key f [--tls-port 443] also serve HTTPS Use the wallet from another computer or phone: HTTPS Browsers only enable wallet cryptography on secure pages : https://… (or localhost ). If other devices open your node's address over plain http:// , the wallet cannot create or sign anything (the browser disables it). Two ways to fix that: A real domain (best): put the node behind Caddy ( deploy/Caddyfile ), which gets a trusted certificate automatically. Visitors need nothing. Your own certificate for a private network: create one, start with --tls-cert/--tls-key , and install that certificate as trusted on each device. A self-signed certificate is refused by browsers until you do; AUREN cannot and will not bypass that. `` bash openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -keyout key.pem -out cert.pem -days 365 -subj "/CN=192.168.1.20" -addext "subjectAltName=IP:192.168.1.20" ./auren join testnet --public --tls-cert cert.pem --tls-key key.pem --tls-port 9660 `` (Verified: the HTTPS listener serves the API, wallet page and RPC. A browser accepting the certificate is on your side.) Keep it running Windows: Install-AUREN.ps1 can create a sign-in task. Remove it with schtasks /Delete /TN "AUREN Node (testnet)" /F . Linux: deploy/auren-node.service (systemd). Use ExecStart=/usr/bin/node bin/auren.js join testnet . Android: Termux keeps running with a wake lock ( termux-wake-lock ); disable battery optimization for Termux. Update Download the newest package and unpack it over (or beside) the old one. Your data in ~/.auren is separate and is kept. Never mix data between networks. Becoming a validator (advanced) A regular node checks the network, and with --earn it also earns AUR (see node-rewards.md ). Validators also propose and sign blocks and earn rewards, and putting their stake at risk. Read docs/validators.md first: you will create a separate consensus key, stake AUR, and must never run two nodes with the same key (that is slashed). Back up Your wallet seed phrase is the only copy of your funds. Node data ( ~/.auren/<network> ) can always be re-downloaded from the network; do back up priv_validator_key.json if you run a validator. h: Account protection | Daily limit | Timelocked loosening | Guardian recovery | Simulation | Keys | Post-quantum readiness | What we do not claim | Operational checklist (validators)
x: Security architecture Layered, because no single feature is "the" security. Layer Mechanism Where Consensus one-vote-per-height rule, double-sign evidence, slashing, jailing, power cap consensus.js , chain.js Transactions chain ID in signed bytes, sequential nonces, Ed25519 signatures, fee pre-checks tx.js Execution fixed deterministic costs, block resource limits, failure isolation (fork per tx) tx.js , chain.js Accounts daily limits, timelocks, guardians, recovery tx.js Keys scrypt + AES-256-GCM keystore, separate operator and consensus keys crypto.js , client.js Network rate-limited RPC, body-size caps, peer genesis check node.js Upgrades published proposals + timelock (Phase 2) n/a yet Account protection Daily limit setSecurity.dailyLimit caps the sum of transfer amounts per window ( limitWindowBlocks , 1 day on mainnet). Staking, claiming and name fees are not "withdrawals" and do not count. Timelocked loosening A setSecurity call that is at least as strict as the current configuration (same guardians, threshold and delay not lower, limit not higher) applies immediately. Anything looser is queued for delayBlocks . Any guardian, or the account itself, can cancel the queued change ( securityCancel ). Guardian recovery Owner sets 1-9 guardians and a threshold with setSecurity (delay ≥ protocol minimum). If the key is lost, each guardian submits recoveryApprove{account, newPub} . A guardian proposing a different new key resets the approvals. At threshold the recovery becomes ready after delayBlocks . The owner can recoveryCancel within that window. When ready, the account's authPub becomes newPub : the old key stops working, and the account's address, balance and nonce stay the same. Limit of the design: recovery is for lost keys. If a thief holds the key, they can cancel a recovery. What bounds that case is the daily limit and the guardian veto on loosening. Simulation aur_simulate (or aurenctl … --simulate ) runs the transaction against a fork of current state and returns ok , error code, fee, burn, and the exact before/after of every touched account, so a wallet can show "you will send X and pay Y" before signing. It is as accurate as the next block; fees can change by ≤ 12.5% per block. Keys Operator key (holds funds, creates the validator, claims rewards): keep offline / hardware-backed when hardware-wallet support lands. Encrypted keystore at ~/.auren/keystore (override with AUREN_KEYSTORE ). Consensus key ( priv_validator_key.json , signs votes only): lives on the validator host, mode 0600. It can never move funds. Losing it costs availability; duplicating it costs 5% of stake. Never run two nodes with one consensus key. The faucet and devnet keys are public by design. Post-quantum readiness Addresses embed a scheme byte; transactions will carry a scheme-tagged signature. Scheme 1 is reserved for ML-DSA (FIPS 204). We will not force large signatures on all transactions: the plan is to (1) benchmark signature size, verification time and bandwidth on a testnet, (2) let accounts opt in, (3) revisit defaults as the threat becomes concrete. Until then, Ed25519 is the only implemented scheme. What we do not claim No formal verification, no audit. The conservation invariant, lane-independence property and commit-quorum rules are tested, not proven. P2P is plain HTTP (see consensus.md#known-limitations ). The node trusts its own disk: a corrupted block log is detected by replay verification, but there is no snapshot signature scheme. Operational checklist (validators) Run exactly one instance per consensus key; no hot standby sharing the key. Firewall the RPC ( --rpc-host 127.0.0.1 + reverse proxy with TLS and rate limits for public RPC). Monitor /metrics : auren_block_height , auren_catching_up , auren_peers . Back up priv_validator_key.json offline and data/priv_validator_state.json with the node. Keep operator keys off the validator host.

x: Deploy a smart contract AUREN runs an Ethereum-compatible virtual machine, so the tools you already know work. Connect your tools Devnet Testnet Mainnet RPC URL http://NODE:9650/rpc a testnet node a mainnet node Chain ID 77001 77002 77000 Currency AUR AUR AUR In MetaMask: add a network with the RPC URL and chain ID above. Your Ethereum address ( 0x… ) is also an AUREN account, so a key you use on Ethereum works here. Units An EVM account balance is shown in wei . 1 AUR = 10^18 wei in the EVM, and 1 AUR = 10^9 sparks natively. The conversion is automatic: tools see 18 decimals. Hardhat ethers Fund the address first by sending it AUR from a wallet (an Ethereum address works as an AUREN account). From the command line What is supported AUREN runs the Shanghai version of the Ethereum virtual machine. The standard precompiled contracts 1 to 5 and 9 are available; the pairing-curve precompiles (6 to 8) are not. The interpreter was compared against the reference implementation on thousands of programs. Details and limits: EVM . Fees A contract call pays for the gas it uses, in AUR, at the current fee level. The wallet or tool estimates gas for you ( eth_estimateGas ). Unused gas is refunded. Fees are burned. Tips Test on the devnet first; it resets and is free. Verify addresses and chain ID before sending. A wrong chain ID makes a transaction invalid, which protects you from replay on other networks. Contract calls run one after another, not in parallel, so heavy use of contracts competes for the same block space.

h: How it works | Choosing a validator | Risks | Rewards | Run your own validator
x: Staking guide Staking means locking your AUR to back a validator. Validators run the computers that confirm payments. In return, new AUR is shared with the validators and everyone who staked with them. How it works You choose a validator in the wallet's Stake tab and enter an amount. Your coins are locked. They still belong to you. Rewards build up as blocks are confirmed. Press Claim to move them to your balance. To get your coins back, press Unstake . They return after a waiting period (the "unbonding" period; 28 days by default on mainnet), shown under Coming back to you . Choosing a validator Look at three things in the table: Share of network. Spreading stake across many validators makes the network safer. Pick one that is not already huge. No validator can have more than a capped share of the voting power. Fee cut (commission). The part of your rewards the validator keeps. Status. Avoid ones marked paused (they missed too many blocks) or banned (they cheated and were penalised). Risks Penalties. If your validator cheats (signs two different blocks at the same height), part of the stake behind it is cut and burned. Pause-level mistakes such as long downtime have a smaller penalty. Choose reliable validators. Waiting period. You cannot spend staked coins until the unbonding period ends. Unaudited software. AUREN has not been independently audited yet. Only stake what you can afford to lose. Rewards New AUR is issued each block (3% a year at the start, falling by 15% a year down to a floor of 0.5%). 10% of it goes to the node-reward pool ( Node rewards ) and the rest to validators and the people who staked with them, after validator commission. Fees paid by users are burned, not paid out. Details: Tokenomics . Run your own validator If you want to run a validator yourself, read Validators . It needs a larger stake and a reliable computer.

x: Start here Welcome. This page gets you from nothing to using AUREN in about ten minutes. No technical knowledge needed. What AUREN is AUREN is a public network with its own coin, AUR . You can send AUR to anyone in seconds for a tiny fee, earn rewards by staking it, give your wallet an easy name like alice.aur , and use apps built on it. Independent computers (nodes) check every payment, so no single company controls it. What you need A web browser. That is all. Or download the AUREN Wallet app for Windows or Android from the releases page . Step 1: Open your wallet Go to the website and press Open wallet (or open the app). Pick a network at the top: Devnet , Testnet or Mainnet . See Networks for what each one is. Mainnet has not launched yet. Step 2: Create your wallet Press Create a new wallet . Save your recovery key. Write it on paper and keep it somewhere safe. It is the only way to get your coins back if you forget your password or lose your device. Never share it with anyone. Nobody from AUREN will ever ask for it. Choose a password. You will type it each time you open the wallet on this device. Details for every option: Wallet guide . Step 3: Get some AUR On the devnet and testnet, open Receive and press Get 1,000 AUR . Coins arrive in a few seconds. On mainnet you will get AUR by receiving it from someone else. Step 4: Send a payment Open Send . Enter an address or a name like alice.aur , and an amount. Press Review . The wallet asks the network to preview the payment and shows the exact fee. A normal payment costs a tiny fraction of a cent. Press Sign & send . It confirms in a few seconds. Step 5: Receive a payment Open Receive and copy your address. Share it with the person paying you. It is safe to share. Step 6: Earn by staking Open Stake , pick a validator, enter an amount and confirm. You earn rewards while it is staked. When you unstake, your coins come back after a waiting period. Read the Staking guide first. Step 7: Get a name Open Names , search a name like alice , and register it. Now people can pay alice.aur instead of a long address. You can even create your own ending, like .david . See Names, domains and your own TLD . Step 8: Help the network and earn Run a node on your computer or phone and earn a share of new AUR. Download AUREN Node , choose a network, keep Earn AUR on and press Start . See Run a node and Node rewards . Staying safe AUREN is new software and has not been independently audited yet. Only use what you can afford to lose. Keep your recovery key private and offline. Check the address and amount on the Review screen every time. Set up trusted helpers and a daily limit in Security ( Wallet guide ). Where next I want to... x: Tokenomics Everything marked (proposed) is a starting assumption for public discussion before mainnet. The code implements the mechanisms; the numbers live in genesis and can change before launch. Asset Name / symbol AUREN / AUR (working names) Decimals 9 (1 AUR = 1,000,000,000 sparks) Roles pays fees, staked for security, weights governance (Phase 2) Cap none; issuance is rule-based and tapers Supply mechanics Who receives issuance: validators that signed the previous block, pro rata to voting power; each validator splits it between commission and delegators via the reward index. Burned: base fees, slashed stake, .aur registration fees. Not burned: tips (to the proposer) and unclaimed rewards (they accrue to delegators). Year Issuance rate 1 3.00% 2 2.55% 3 2.17% 5 1.57% 10 0.69% 13+ 0.50% floor Example: with 1,000,000,000 AUR, year-1 issuance is ≈ 30,000,000 AUR. If fees burn 10,000,000 AUR that year, net growth is 20,000,000 AUR (2.0%). Burning does not guarantee a falling supply or a rising price; it only offsets issuance when usage is high enough. Why a tail emission instead of a hard cap A fixed cap means validator income eventually depends only on fees. If fee revenue is thin, security spend falls with it, which weakens the chain precisely when it is young. A small perpetual floor (0.5%) keeps a predictable security budget while the decaying schedule removes most dilution over time. The trade-off is explicit: AUR is not fixed-supply. If the community prefers a cap, this is the parameter to debate before genesis. Initial distribution (proposed, for discussion) Bucket Share Terms Community, ecosystem & grants 35% released by public programs Validator & staking bootstrap 15% seeds genesis validator stake and early delegations Foundation treasury 20% vested over 4 years Core contributors 15% 1-year cliff, 4-year vesting Early supporters 10% vesting, disclosed terms Security, audits & bug bounty 5% The protocol already supports vesting accounts ( vesting: {total, start, cliff, end} in genesis): locked balance is excluded from spendable and cannot pay fees or be staked until it unlocks. No token sale is part of this repository. Fee flows Staking parameters (mainnet defaults) Max validators 150 Min self-stake 10,000 AUR Voting-power cap 10% of bonded stake per validator Max commission 20% Unbonding 28 days Double-sign 5% slashed, tombstoned Downtime jailed 1 day, 0.1% slashed if absent from > 50% of a window Conservation invariant The test-suite asserts after every scenario: supply = Σ balances + Σ bonded + Σ unbonding + Σ accrued rewards . Any change that mints or burns must keep this exact. Governance of economics Issuance, fee, and slashing parameters may change only through an on-chain proposal with a long timelock and an explicit activation height (Phase 2). Until the governance module exists, parameters are fixed by genesis and change only through a coordinated, publicly announced upgrade.
