x: Troubleshooting The wallet cannot connect Check your internet connection. Pick a network in the selector and press Connect . If the message says there is no public node for that network yet, that network is not reachable right now. Mainnet has not launched. You can run your own node ( Run a node ) or choose Custom node… and enter the address of one. "That password did not work" Passwords are case-sensitive. If you really forgot it, choose Add another wallet → I already have a wallet and enter your recovery key with a new password. My payment is stuck on "waiting" Blocks arrive every second or two. If the network is busy, add a small Extra tip . If the node you use is behind, wait a moment or choose another node. "would fail" on the review screen The network previewed your payment and it would not work. Common reasons: not enough balance (remember the fee), a name that does not exist, or a daily limit you set. The review screen shows the reason. You are not charged for a payment you do not send. A name is refused as "ambiguous" Two networks give that name to different addresses. The wallet refuses to pay so you cannot pay the wrong person. Use the address instead. The faucet says "refused" You may have asked too often. Wait a little and try again, or use a different address. The faucet exists only on the devnet and testnet. The device-key option is greyed out Your browser cannot use device keys here. Device keys need a secure page (HTTPS or the local app) and a supported browser. The Windows and Android wallet apps run on a secure local address, so they work. Windows says it protects my PC The apps are not code-signed. Choose More info , then Run anyway . You can compare the file to the one on the releases page . The Android app will not install Allow installs from this source when Android asks. The node app needs a 64-bit phone and a few hundred MB of space. The node will not start Check you chose the right network. If you see a message about genesis, you may have old data from another chain. Use a new data folder ( --home ). A devnet on your computer is reachable from a phone only at your computer's network address, not 127.0.0.1 . x: Running a validator Works the same on testnet and (eventually) mainnet; only the network name and the money differ. 1. Requirements Node.js 20+, a dedicated Linux host (2+ cores, 4 GB RAM, SSD), a stable public IP or port-forward, accurate clock (use chrony /NTP). Two keys: an operator key (funds, kept in a keystore) and a consensus key (created by auren-node init , signs votes). Stake: at least minSelfStake (mainnet default 10,000 AUR; testnet via the faucet). 2. Initialize Edit /var/lib/auren/config.json : add seed peers , and set rpcHost to 127.0.0.1 (put TLS + rate limiting in front if you serve public RPC). Leave operator as null until step 4. 3. Start as a full node and let it sync A systemd unit is in deploy/auren-node.service . 4. Create the validator on-chain Now set "operator": "<your operator address>" in config.json and restart the node. It starts voting once it is in the active set (next block after your stake lands and exceeds minSelfStake ). 5. Operate Task Command Am I active? aurenctl status → validator.active ; aurenctl validators Claim rewards + commission aurenctl claim <your operator address> --from operator Add stake aurenctl delegate <operator address> <amount> --from operator Leave aurenctl undelegate <operator address> <amount> --from operator ; funds return after unbonding Unjail after downtime aurenctl validator unjail --from operator (after jailBlocks ) 6. Rules that cost money if broken Never run two nodes with the same consensus key. That is double signing: 5% slashed, tombstoned forever. This includes "failover" setups and restoring a backup while the old node is alive. Always keep data/priv_validator_state.json with the node. If you migrate hosts, copy it too and stop the old node first. Downtime: missing > 50% of a window jails you; you also forgo rewards when you are not signing. Keep the operator key off the validator host. 7. Monitoring GET /metrics (Prometheus): auren_block_height , auren_catching_up , auren_peers , auren_mempool_size , auren_base_fee_* , auren_active_validators , auren_nakamoto_* . Alert on: height not advancing for > 30 s, catching_up == 1 , peers == 0. 8. Decentralization etiquette The chain measures voting-power concentration but cannot see hosting. Please avoid the largest cloud region among current validators, publish your jurisdiction and operator identity if you can, and do not split one entity into many validators to take more power.

x: Wallet guide A tour of every screen in the AUREN wallet (website, Windows app and Android app). Connecting At the top you pick a network: Devnet , Testnet , Mainnet , or Custom node… (for people who run their own node; it reveals an address box). The tag next to the title shows which network you are on. If a network is not reachable, the wallet says so instead of switching silently. Making or adding a wallet The first screen offers three choices, one step per page: Create a new wallet. Step 1 shows your recovery key. Step 2 asks you to choose a name and a password. I already have a wallet. Paste your recovery key and choose a new password for this device. Use my phone or security key. The key lives inside your device (fingerprint, face, Windows Hello or a hardware key). Every payment needs your touch. If you lose the device you lose the wallet, so add trusted helpers in Security first. Your wallet is locked with your password and stays on this device. Nothing secret is ever sent anywhere. The main screen The big number is your spendable balance . Under it you see what is staked, rewards waiting for you, coins coming back from unstaking, and anything locked. Four buttons cover everyday use; more tabs sit below them. Send Enter an address or a name ( alice.aur , alice.david ) and an amount. Names are checked on your device. If a name could belong to different people on different networks the wallet refuses to pay until you are sure. Review shows the fee and what will change, and asks the network to preview the payment. You confirm to sign and send. The optional Extra tip pays a little more to go first when the network is busy. Leave it as is normally. Receive Your address, with Copy address . On the devnet and testnet there is also Get 1,000 AUR . Stake Back a validator to earn rewards. Choose one, enter an amount, confirm. Your stake lists what you staked and your rewards (press to claim). Unstaking returns your coins after a waiting period, shown under Coming back to you . See the Staking guide . Activity Your recent payments, with their result and fee. Each links to the explorer. Names Search and register names like alice.aur , point a name at an address, set your primary name (shown when people look up your address), and manage a name you own. You can also create your own name ending such as .david and set its price. See Names, domains and your own TLD . Vote Anyone who stakes can vote on proposals that change network settings. Votes count in proportion to stake. Security Trusted helpers: addresses of people or other wallets that can help you recover your account if you lose your key. You choose how many must agree. Waiting time: a delay before weaker settings apply, so a thief cannot loosen your protection at once. Any helper can cancel it. Daily limit: the most that can leave your account per day. This limits the damage if someone gets your key. Help someone recover: if you are a trusted helper for someone, approve moving their account to their new key. Backup Show your recovery key again (needs your password), or remove this wallet from this device. Removing it without a saved recovery key loses access to your coins for good. Safety checklist Keep your recovery key offline and private. Check the address and amount every time. Set a daily limit and trusted helpers. The wallet locks itself after 10 minutes of inactivity. Problems? See Troubleshooting .

h: 1. Motivation | 2. Architecture | 3. Consensus (summary; full spec in consensus.md) | 4. Adaptive Execution Market (summary; fee-market.md) | 5. Monetary policy (summary; tokenomics.md) | 6. Native account security (security.md) | 7. Interoperability (design only) | 8. Governance | 9. Threat model and known gaps | 10. References
x: AUREN Whitepaper (v0.1, draft) An independent Layer 1 built around verifiable security, predictable cost and protocol-level account protection. Draft for discussion. Parameters marked (proposed) are starting assumptions, not commitments. AUREN/AUR are working names. 1. Motivation Most new chains compete on headline throughput and low fees. Those numbers are easy to claim and hard to compare, and they say little about what users actually experience: fees that spike unpredictably, validator sets that quietly centralize, and accounts whose safety depends entirely on a wallet app. AUREN pursues four goals and tries to measure each one: Verifiable security : finality, slashing evidence and upgrade history are checkable from the chain itself. Predictable performance : bounded blocks, fixed per-operation resource costs, fees that cannot move more than 12.5% per block. Validator accessibility : requirements a normal operator can meet, with decentralization measured (Nakamoto coefficient) rather than asserted. Predictable monetary policy : a published issuance schedule and a burned base fee, with no discretionary inflation. None of these ideas is new in isolation (BFT PoS, EIP-1559-style pricing, delegated staking, guardian recovery all exist elsewhere). The contribution is the specific combination, the rules written down precisely, and a reference implementation with tests that anyone can run. We make no "world first" claim. 2. Architecture Modules: consensus, execution, fee engine, staking, state store, and optional name service. The name module is separate by construction: if it fails, transfers and consensus are unaffected. 3. Consensus (summary; full spec in consensus.md ) Validators are the top N (default 150) by bonded stake, with a per-validator voting-power cap (default 10% of total bonded stake; effective once the set is large enough). For each (height, round) a proposer is drawn deterministically in proportion to voting power. It builds a block, executes it, and commits to the post-state root. Each validator re-executes the block, and signs at most one block per height , persisting the vote before sending it. A block with votes from more than ⅔ of voting power is final. The certificate is embedded in the next block. Safety: two conflicting finalized blocks require ≥ ⅓ of power to have signed twice at one height, which is provable and slashed (5%, permanent ejection). The current implementation is single-phase; the roadmap replaces it with a two-round protocol with proof-of-lock (see limitations). 4. Adaptive Execution Market (summary; fee-market.md ) Resources are split into compute and state . Every transaction type has a fixed cost in each. A transaction pays cost_compute × baseFee_compute + cost_state × baseFee_state , which is burned , plus an optional tip to the proposer. Each base fee updates per block toward 50% utilization: Transactions declare the state keys they touch. A lane scheduler groups them with union-find: independent transactions land in different lanes, conflicting ones share a lane in block order. Fees, burns and tips are settled at end of block, so lanes never contend for shared accounts. Lane order provably does not change the final state root (randomized test). This combines known ideas (multi-dimensional fee markets, declared access sets, EIP-1559). Whether it beats alternatives is an empirical question the benchmarks in scripts/ are meant to answer. 5. Issuance: 3.0% annually, decaying 15% per year to a 0.5% floor (proposed) . Minted per block, only for validators that signed the previous block, split with delegators. Burn: all base fees, slashed stake, and name-registration fees. Net supply change = issuance − burn. Burning does not by itself create value; demand, circulation and rewards matter. No hard cap: a tail emission funds security as block rewards shrink. Parameter changes require a public on-chain proposal, a long timelock and an explicit activation height. 6. Native account security ( security.md ) Daily limit enforced in the state machine. Tightening is instant; loosening is queued behind a timelock and any guardian can veto it. Guardian recovery: up to 9 guardians and a threshold. Approvals start a delay; the owner can cancel. After the delay the account's authorizing key changes. Scheme 0 is Ed25519; scheme 1 is reserved for ML-DSA (NIST FIPS 204). Adoption follows benchmarking of signature size, verification speed and bandwidth. What this does not do: recovery handles lost keys. Against an attacker holding the key, the daily limit and guardian veto bound the loss; they do not eliminate it. 7. Interoperability (design only) Every block carries its parent's >⅔ certificate, so a light client can follow the chain by verifying signatures against a known validator set. A bridge must specify: how it verifies the other chain, what happens when the verifier or relayer fails, and when and how assets can be recovered. We will not ship a bridge without those three written down and reviewed. 8. Governance Phase 2. Proposals, voting weighted by stake, long timelock, activation heights, and an emergency path limited to halting block production (never to changing balances). 9. x: Contributing Thanks for helping. A few rules keep a consensus-critical codebase healthy. Ground rules Determinism is sacred. Anything reachable from executeBlock must produce identical results on every node: no Date.now() , Math.random() , floating-point math, or iteration over unsorted maps. Use BigInt for amounts. Every state key a transaction touches must be in its access set ( src/tx.js ). The lane scheduler relies on it. test/core.test.js runs a randomized lane-order test; extend it when you add a transaction type. Conservation must hold. assertConserved() in the tests checks supply == balances + bonded + unbonding + accrued rewards . New minting or burning paths need a test that keeps it green. Consensus changes need a spec change in docs/ in the same pull request, plus a note in CHANGELOG.md . Zero runtime dependencies. Prefer node: built-ins. Discuss before adding one. Workflow Keep pull requests small and focused; include tests that fail without your change. Code style: CommonJS, 'use strict' , 2-space indent, comments explain why . x: Security policy AUREN is unaudited, pre-testnet software . Do not use it to hold value. Reporting a vulnerability Please report privately; do not open a public issue for anything that could affect a running network. Set a monitored security contact (e.g. security@<your-domain> ) before any public testnet and replace this line. Include: affected component, a reproduction (a failing test is ideal), and the impact you believe it has. Targets we care most about: consensus safety (two finalized blocks at one height), state-root divergence between honest nodes, inflation/minting bugs (the token-conservation invariant is tested in test/core.test.js ), signature or replay bypass, mempool/RPC denial of service, and keystore weaknesses. Scope and rules of engagement Test against your own local devnet ( npm run devnet ). Never test against third-party nodes without permission. Give us reasonable time to fix before disclosure. A bug bounty is planned for the public testnet phase. What the project commits to Security-relevant protocol changes are published as proposals with a timelock before activation.
